text:
Pierre, with a meek smile of regret and repentance, his legs and arms spread helplessly apart, stood squarely before Dolokhov with his broad chest and looked at him sadly. Denisov, Rostov, and Nesvitsky screwed their eyes shut. At one and the same moment they heard a shot and Dolokhov’s angry cry.

“Missed!” shouted Dolokhov, and collapsed limply, face down, onto the snow. Pierre clutched his head and, turning back, walked toward the woods, planting his whole foot in the snow and repeating incomprehensible words aloud:

“Stupid... stupid! Death... lies...” he kept saying, wincing. Nesvitsky stopped him and took him home.

Rostov and Denisov took the wounded Dolokhov away.

Dolokhov lay silent in the sleigh with his eyes closed and did not answer a word to the questions put to him; but upon entering Moscow, he suddenly came to and, raising his head with difficulty, took the hand of Rostov, who was sitting beside him. Rostov was struck by the utterly changed and unexpectedly ecstatic and tender expression on Dolokhov’s face.

“Well, how is it? How do you feel?” Rostov asked.

“Bad! But that is not the point. My friend,” Dolokhov said in a faltering voice, “where are we? We are in Moscow, I know. I am nothing, but I have killed her, killed her... She will not bear it. She will not bear it...”

“Who?” Rostov asked.

“My mother. My mother, my angel, my adored angel, Mother,” and Dolokhov began to weep, squeezing Rostov’s hand. When he had calmed down somewhat, he explained to Rostov that he lived with his mother, and that if his mother saw him dying, she would not bear it. He implored Rostov to go to her and prepare her.

Rostov went on ahead to carry out the errand, and to his great surprise learned that Dolokhov, that rowdy, that duelist Dolokhov, lived in Moscow with his elderly mother and his hunchbacked sister, and was the most tender of sons and brothers.

VI.

Of late Pierre had seldom seen his wife face to face. Both in Petersburg and in Moscow their house was constantly full of guests. On the night after the duel, as he often did, he did not go to the bedroom but remained in his enormous father’s study, the very room in which Count Bezukhov had died.

He lay down on the sofa and wanted to fall asleep so as to forget everything that had happened to him, but he could not do so. Such a storm of feelings, thoughts, and memories suddenly arose in his soul that not only could he not sleep, he could not sit still and had to spring up from the sofa and pace rapidly about the room. At one moment he pictured her as she had been in the first days after their marriage, with bare shoulders and a weary, passionate gaze, and immediately beside her there appeared Dolokhov’s handsome, insolent, firmly mocking face as it had been at the dinner, and then that same face of Dolokhov, pale, trembling, and suffering, as it had been when he turned and fell onto the snow.

“What happened?” he asked himself. “I killed my wife’s lover, yes, killed my wife’s lover. Yes, that is what happened. Why? How did I come to this?” “Because you married her,” an inner voice replied.

“But what am I guilty of?” he asked. “Of marrying her without loving her, of deceiving both yourself and her”—and there arose vividly before him that moment after supper at Prince Vasily’s when he had uttered those words that had not come from within him: “I love you.” “It all came from that! Even then I felt,” he thought, “I felt then that it was not right, that I had no right to it. And so it turned out.” He remembered their honeymoon and blushed at the memory. Especially vivid, offensive, and shameful to him was the memory of how, one day, soon after his marriage, toward noon, he had come from the bedroom into the study in a silk dressing gown, and in the study had found the chief steward, who bowed respectfully, looked at Pierre’s face and at his dressing gown, and smiled slightly, as though by that smile expressing respectful sympathy with his employer’s happiness.

“And how many times I was proud of her, proud of her majestic beauty, of her social tact,” he thought; “proud of that house of mine in which she received all Petersburg, proud of her inaccessibility and beauty. So that was what I was proud of! I thought then that I did not understand her. How often, pondering her character, I told myself that I was to blame for not understanding her, for not understanding that perpetual composure, contentment, and absence of any passions or desires; but the whole answer lay in that terrible phrase: that she was a depraved woman. I spoke that terrible phrase to myself, and everything became clear!

“Anatole used to go to her to borrow money from her and kissed her bare shoulders. She did not give him money, but she allowed him to kiss her. Her father, in jest, tried to arouse her jealousy; with a calm smile she said that she was not so stupid as to be jealous: let him do whatever he wished, she said of me. I once asked her whether she felt any signs of pregnancy. She laughed scornfully and said that she was not a fool who wished to have children, and that she would have no children by me.”

Then he remembered the coarseness and bluntness of her thoughts and the vulgarity of expression characteristic of her despite her upbringing in the highest aristocratic circles. “I’m not some sort of fool... go and try it yourself... go take a walk,” she would say. Often, seeing her success in the eyes of old and young men and women, Pierre could not understand why he did not love her. “Why, I never loved her,” Pierre told himself; “I knew she was a depraved woman,” he repeated to himself, “but I did not dare admit it.”

“And now Dolokhov—there he sits on the snow, forcing himself to smile, and perhaps dying, responding to my remorse with some sort of feigned bravado!”

Pierre was one of those people who, despite their outward, so-called weakness of character, do not seek a confidant for their grief. He worked through his grief alone within himself.

“She alone is to blame for everything, everything,” he told himself; “but what of it? Why did I bind myself to her, why did I say to her that ‘I love you,’ which was a lie and worse than a lie?” he told himself. “I am guilty and must bear... What? The disgrace to my name, the misery of my life? Ah, it is all nonsense,” he thought, “the disgrace to my name and honor too; it is all conventional, all independent of me.

“Louis XVI was executed because they said that he was dishonorable and a criminal,” it occurred to Pierre, “and from their point of view they were right, just as those who died martyrs’ deaths for him and numbered him among the saints were right. Then Robespierre was executed because he was a despot. Who is right, who is guilty? No one. Live and let live: tomorrow you will die, as I might have died an hour ago. And is it worth suffering when one has only a single second left to live compared with eternity?” But at the very moment when he believed himself calmed by reasoning of this kind, he would suddenly picture her at those moments when he had most strongly displayed his insincere love for her, and he felt the blood surge to his heart, and had to get up again, move about, and break and tear whatever objects came to hand. “Why did I say to her, ‘I love you’?” he kept repeating to himself. And after repeating that question for the tenth time, Molière’s words occurred to him: “But what the devil was he doing in that galley?” and he laughed at himself.
